verdict: Avoid new unsecured or greenfield exposure in Vadodara chemicals; lend selectively only to established, export-contracted units with tight structure and monthly data.
title: Vadodara Chemicals, Dyes & Intermediates: a note to the credit manager
narrative:
## What this business physically is
Vadodara runs on small and mid-sized chemical units converting basic feedstock into dyes, intermediates and specialty chemicals, sold to textile, pharma and agro buyers at home and abroad. **Cash is made on conversion spread and volume throughput, not on price** — most units pass input costs through with a lag, so margin lives in the lag and in capacity utilisation. The city is dense: over 1,000 chemical industries sit around Vadodara [2], which means cluster-level safety and environmental risk is a real credit factor, not a footnote. ## What has changed now
**The macro backdrop is against us: IIP chemicals output is -0.5% YoY and -1.2% Apr-to-date [D], while bank credit to the sector is running +20.7% YoY [D]** — a 21.9 pp gap between money lent and goods made [D]. That gap is the single most important fact in this note: the system is lending into a flat-output industry. Brent at $113/bbl sits above the $75–100 band [D], which squeezes feedstock-linked units that cannot reprice fast enough. Against that, the peer read is genuinely strong: Aarti Industries posted record quarterly revenue and EBITDA, PAT up 60% to Rs. 169 crore on 30% volume growth [4], with revenue up 75% to Rs. 3,668 crore [5]. **Read this correctly — the winners are export-contracted, volume-led specialty players, not the general cluster.** Rating commentary flags elevated working-capital intensity in high-growth phases [8] and a prior year of 9% revenue dip on Chinese dumping and de-stocking [7]; both are undated, so weight them as pattern, not current fact. ## Where to grow
**Pursue established specialty and dye-intermediate units with signed export or long-term supply contracts, visible volume growth, and a demonstrated pass-through mechanism** — the Aarti-type profile [3][5]. Pursue ancillary units supplying these exporters. **Avoid commodity alkalies, single-product dye units with no contract cover, and any greenfield or expansion proposal in the current credit-vs-output gap.** When a proposal lands, check the customer's contract tenor and pass-through clause first; if pricing is spot-only, ask for the last four quarters of gross margin to see whether they actually recovered input costs. ## How to grow safely
**Structure on cash conversion, not on turnover.** Take monthly stock-and-debtor statements, quarterly GSTR-2B vs purchase reconciliation, and a monthly capacity-utilisation figure. Because working capital blocks cash in growth [8], set the drawing power on a tighter debtor-and-inventory margin than usual. Ask for the pollution-control consent validity and the unit's safety audit status — in a 1,000-unit cluster [2], a single incident can freeze a borrower's operations. Collect from customer: current order book, export share, and feedstock contract tenure. ## Early warning signs
- **Utilisation falling below the level at sanction for two consecutive months** — ask for the order book and whether contracts have been repriced. - **Debtor days stretching while sales are flat** — this is the classic sign of pushing stock into the channel; cut drawing power. - **Any regulatory or safety notice at the unit or its immediate cluster** — stop fresh disbursement until cleared.
watch: Monthly capacity utilisation and stock statement
Two consecutive months below sanction level -> ask for order book and hold fresh disbursement
Mismatch above 5% of purchases -> seek explanation and reprice limit
Quarterly gross margin and debtor days
Margin compression with rising debtor days -> reduce drawing power
Consent to operate / safety audit status (quarterly)
Any lapse or notice -> freeze limit until cleared
Sustained above $100/bbl [D] -> test pass-through clause on top exposures
